description:
We are The Space Commanders, a family team made up of a mother, her two sons, and their uncle.

We all love science, technology, and space exploration. We enjoy working together, learning new things, and trying to turn our ideas into real projects.

We each bring different skills and ideas to the team, but what makes this experience special is that we get to do it together as a family, have fun, and learn along the way.
summary:
Junior Space Commander is a game designed by kids, for kids, where players take charge of a Mars base for five sols (Martian days). Their mission is to keep the crew safe while balancing limited resources like power, food, radiation protection, and crew health.
But surviving on Mars isn't easy. Every decision involves trade-offs. Reducing power to the greenhouse saves energy but affects food production. Adding radiation shielding protects the astronauts but uses more power. Sending a rover on a longer mission brings back more scientific discoveries but costs battery and puts the crew at risk. Choices made today can affect the mission tomorrow.
Through interactive missions, challenges, and mini-games, kids explore real NASA science. The game uses NASA's DONKI space weather data to introduce real solar events, while mini-games inspired by NASA OSDR studies let kids learn about bone loss, growing plants on Mars, radiation, and DNA repair.
Our goal is to make space science fun and accessible. Instead of just reading about the challenges of space exploration, kids get to make their own decisions, experiment, learn from their mistakes, and try different strategies.
details:
Junior Space Commander is a browser-interactive game. Kids run Astro Base, a Mars outpost, for five sols (Martian days). They lead four astronauts: Max the engineer, Elsa the doctor, Charles the scientist and Lea the botanist. The goal is to keep four resources healthy: power, radiation shielding, food and crew health.

Each sol starts with a crisis that is decided at the Command Center: a power overload, a dust storm on the solar panels, a frozen greenhouse, a solar radiation storm and a choice of rover route. Every option shows its cost before the player picks it, and no option is free. Dimming the greenhouse saves power but means less food. Extra shielding protects the crew but drains power. A long rover trip earns more science but costs battery and health. The effects carry over from one sol to the next, so a choice that saves power today can hurt the crew tomorrow.

Players then walk each astronaut to their station to do hands-on tasks. There are 20 mini-games, including wiring, frozen pipes, radiation badges, a bone scan, a greenhouse investigation, a DNA repair puzzle, and two 3D rover drives. Some of these mini-games are inspired by real NASA research experiments, allowing kids to explore scientific concepts through play. On the last sol, the crew sends a report to Earth over a sped-up Mars–Earth radio link. This shows why astronauts can’t always wait for answers and have to make decisions on their own.

A dashboard with dials, warning lights and trends shows the state of the base. The pictures change too: day and night, dust, damaged equipment and the condition of the crops. Rocky, a friendly robot, gives spoken hints and quizzes that unlock as kids make discoveries. The final score is based on science points, completed tasks and the resources left at the end.

What are its benefits?

  • Kids explore the kinds of trade-offs real space mission planners face, explained in plain words.
  • Kids learn about real NASA science and research experiments through hands-on mini-games and challenges.
  • The learning loop is “observe → choose → act → check the result,” so kids learn by doing instead of just reading facts.
  • It runs in any browser with no download or account, and works with touch and keyboard.
  • Two modes: Explorer is forgiving for younger players, while Commander has tighter resources for older kids, siblings, or classrooms.

What impact do you hope it has?
We want kids to come away able to explain a real constraint of living in deep space. For example: “More shielding meant less power, so I had to choose.” We also want them to see that a mission succeeds or fails because of many small decisions, while learning science along the way. By connecting the game to real NASA research and experiments, we hope to spark their curiosity and show them that space science is real, exciting, and still evolving.

What tools, languages and software did you use?

  • JavaScript, Vite, Phaser 3 for the 2D base and three.js for the 3D rover
  • NASA’s DONKI API: Sol 4 shows the strongest solar flare from the last 30 days. If the API isn’t reachable, the game shows the May 2024 X8.7 flare and labels it as a historical example.
  • NASA OSDR studies OSD-980, OSD-412, OSD-581, OSD-346, OSD-964 and OSD-658 are the basis for six science mini-games. RadLab and NASA Mars facts support other lessons, and CSA resources support the food lessons.
  • Tiny Voca speech models for Rocky’s voice, which runs in the browser
  • AI coding assistants helped with code, testing and some artwork. The team designed, directed and playtested the game.
  • No special hardware is needed. It runs on any laptop, tablet or phone with a browser.

How is it creative?

Instead of showing a dashboard of numbers, each resource belongs to a person. Kids walk an astronaut through an illustrated base and fix things with their hands. Real NASA research becomes small puzzles: bending seedlings show how plants respond to gravity, and a letter-matching puzzle shows how DNA repair works. The 3D rover missions add a sense of adventure, letting kids explore the Martian surface while completing science missions. Rocky the robot adds humor, so the game feels like an adventure rather than a test. An Earth/Mars clock shows how a sol slowly drifts away from an Earth day.

Since kids were part of designing the game, we wanted to make sure it was something they would actually enjoy playing and sharing with their friends. That's why we added different mini-games, challenges, and rover adventures to keep players engaged while learning science along the way.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Challenge objectives: We focused on the main goal of the NASA challenge by designing realistic scenarios where kids must make trade-offs between limited resources and understand how their decisions affect the mission.
  • Age and attention: Short tasks, simple language, and science terms like “sol” explained when they first come up.
  • Making science fun: We added puzzles, mini-games, and rover adventures to keep kids engaged while learning science.
  • Honest data: Game numbers are labelled as simulated, NASA sources are linked in the game, and saved data is never presented as live.
  • Accessibility: Reduced motion, volume controls, quieter alerts, and a non-3D option instead of driving.
  • Privacy: No accounts, no chat AI, no microphone, and progress is saved only on the player's device.
  • Playtesting: Our kids were involved in designing and testing the game, and we adjusted the difficulty and gameplay based on their feedback.
